chunk_findings.detail: `own_lapsed` is defined as `existing is not None and existing.holder == holder and cfg.lease.resume_own` — it never checks that the lease actually lapsed. The knob's doc says "The agent whose lease LAPSED resumes it", and the very branch being bypassed distinguishes the two cases (`if existing.expired_at:` with an implied else for a live lease). So a plain `ddflow claim` of an item whose lease is still live and held by the same agent now skips the `reclaim_policy == "report"` handling entirely and falls through to the code path intended for fresh/resumed claims, instead of the existing-lease path. Given a live lease on T1 held by "first" and `resume_own` left at its default `true`, `LC.claim(repo, "T1", agent="first")` bypasses the branch that previously handled "you already hold this", changing behavior for a case the feature never targeted. The condition should also require the lease to be expired (e.g. `existing.expired_at is not None` or equivalent) before short-circuiting.

chunk_findings.detail: `throttled` measures the renewal interval with the wall clock (`time.time()` at lines 47, 50 and 51) rather than a monotonic clock. A backward wall‑clock step — NTP correction, host/VM clock sync after suspend/resume — makes `time.time() - last[0]` decrease (go negative), so the `>= due` guard stays false and `renew()` is never called until the clock has caught back up to the pre‑step value. Concretely: a long `ddflow review` started with `[lease].heartbeat_s = 300` that experiences a 35‑minute backward clock correction will stop renewing for those 35 minutes; with the 30‑minute lease described in the intent, the lease lapses, another agent can claim the overlapping globs (`ddflow/api/**`, golden pins), and the commit hook blocks the item's own commits — exactly the failure this file exists to prevent. Using `time.monotonic()` for the local interval bookkeeping (the lease's `renewed_at` from the state file can still be wall‑clock) removes the dependency on clock steps: elapsed time under `monotonic()` never jumps backwards, so renewal continues at the heartbeat cadence regardless of NTP/suspend adjustments.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasekeep.py:50 (throttled)

chunk_findings.detail: The renewal throttle still decides "is a renewal due" from the wall clock (`time.time()` at 47/50/51), and nothing in this change replaces that with a monotonic reading — the change only swaps `gates.lease_heartbeat` over to `LK.keeper` and advertises the new `lease.renew_long_commands` knob, so the earlier report was left untriaged and its probe is unanswered. Concretely: a 10-minute `ddflow review` (or the 25-minute full-suite gate this feature exists for) started with `lease.heartbeat_s = 300`; an NTP correction or a host/VM suspend-resume steps the wall clock backwards by 35 minutes, so `time.time() - last[0]` goes negative, the `>= due` guard in `throttled` stays false, and `renew()` is never invoked for the rest of the run. The lease then lapses exactly as it did before this change, a second agent leases the overlapping globs (`ddflow/api/**`, golden pins), and the commit hook blocks the item's own commits — the failure mode the change was written to prevent. Using `time.monotonic()` for the interval comparison (and keeping wall time only for reporting) removes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasekeep.py:50 (throttled)

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier MEDIUM finding still holds; this diff does not answer it. `review.py` no longer computes the renewal interval itself, but it hands the very same wall-clock value into the helper: `LK.throttled(renew, it.lease.renewed_at, cfg.lease.heartbeat_s, tick_s)`. `it.lease.renewed_at` is a wall-clock timestamp (the old code compared it against `time.time()`), and nothing in the new `throttled` wrapper shown here changes the clock source to a monotonic one — the triage entry for this finding is `untriaged`, i.e. no fix or probe was supplied. Demonstrating input: a `ddflow review` started with `[lease].heartbeat_s = 300` (default) whose host takes an NTP correction or resumes from suspend, stepping the wall clock backwards by ~35 min. `time.time() - last[0]` then goes negative, so the `>= due` guard in `throttled` stays false and `renew()` is not called for the whole interval the clock needs to catch back up; a 20-minute run therefore still outlives a 30-minute lease, another agent can lease the overlapping globs, and the commit hook blocks the item's own commits — precisely the failure this change exists to prevent. The blast radius is also wider than before, because `pins regenerate` now routes through the same `LK.throttled`/`for_holder` machinery (`_lease_tick` in `pin_files.py`), so it inherits the identical wall-clock dependency. A monotonic reference (`time.monotonic()`, or a fixed run start) is required for the interval guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasekeep.py:47-51 (reached via ddflow/api/review.py:221 and ddflow/api/pin_files.py:_lease_tick)

chunk_findings.detail: The heartbeat is now measured on `time.monotonic()`, but the deadline it is protecting is wall-clock: `for_holder` decides liveness with `time.time()` and the lease's TTL/`renewed_at` are wall-clock. On Linux and macOS `time.monotonic()` (CLOCK_MONOTONIC / `mach_absolute_time`) deliberately does **not** advance while the host is suspended, so after a suspend the throttle under-counts elapsed real time and defers the next renewal by up to `heartbeat_s` of *monotonic* time — which is `heartbeat_s` + the suspend duration of wall time. Concrete input: a `ddflow review` running with `[lease].heartbeat_s = 300`, `ttl_s = 1800`, driven through `throttled(k, renewed_at, 300, tick_s)` with a tick smaller than the heartbeat (e.g. `tick_s = 30`, the case the parameter exists for, giving `due = 270`); the command renews at t=0 and the laptop then suspends for 27 minutes. On resume, wall time says the lease is 27 min old (3 min of TTL left) but `monotonic()` says only seconds have passed since the renewal, so `monotonic() - last[0]` is far below `due` and no renewal is issued; the lease therefore lapses at ~30 min wall time while the process is still running, and the item's own commits are blocked by the reclaim — exactly what DX-lease-renew-in-long-commands set out to prevent. The pre-fix wall-clock guard renewed on the first tick after resume, so this is a regression in the resume case rather than the NTP case (the comment "a clock step (NTP, resume) never stalls the renewals" is only true for a *backward* step). chunk_findings.detail: The change introduces `[lease] renew_long_commands` (default `True`) whose own doc promises the off-switch: "Off: nothing renews during a command and the agent heartbeats itself." chunk_findings.detail: `throttled` anchors the monotonic clock to the wall clock of the *last renewal* by subtracting `max(0.0, time.time() - wall0)`. When the wall clock has stepped backwards since that renewal (`time.time() < renewed_at`), the delta is negative and is clamped to 0, so `mono0` is set to the *current* monotonic time instead of the (later) true monotonic time of the renewal. Both `last[0]` and `last[1]` therefore under-count the elapsed time, and the first renewal is deferred rather than fired immediately — the exact opposite of the neighbouring comment "a step in one can only make the other fire, never both stall." Concrete case with `heartbeat_s=600`, `tick_s=60` (so `due=540`, as any caller passing a poll interval smaller than the heartbeat, e.g. review's ticker, can produce): lease last renewed at wall `T`; the agent works ~25 min (`X=1500s`) before starting the long command at `T+1500`; during that window the wall clock steps back by 2000s. At construction `time.time() - wall0 = 1500 - 2000 = -500`, clamped to 0 ⇒ computed elapsed 0 ⇒ neither condition is due. The first renewal then happens at `construction + due ≈ T+2040s`, while the true elapsed at construction (1500s) already exceeded `due`, so the correct behaviour is to renew immediately. With a 1800s TTL the lease lapses at `T+1800` even though the long command is running and ticking, i.e. the deployed clock-recovery logic produces the very lease lapse this change exists to prevent. (Note this path is only live when `due > 0`; for `for_holder`, which passes `tick_s = heartbeat_s`, `due = 0` and the condition is unconditionally true, masking it.)

Both clocks run from there, so there is no stall beyond one heartbeat. tests/test_lease_keep_long_commands.py throttle tests cover the backward step and the suspend
